## 1. Business Question

About a quarter of the customers in this telecom dataset (26.6%) left the company in the last month. This analysis asks three questions:

1.  Which customers are most likely to churn?
2.  What factors are associated with churn?
3.  How can the company target its retention budget?

## 2. Data

The data is the public IBM Telco Customer Churn sample: about 7,000 customers with their account details, services and whether they left in the last month.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(ranger)
set.seed(2026)

data_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/telco-customer-churn-on-icp4d/master/data/Telco-Customer-Churn.csv"
data_path <- "data/Telco-Customer-Churn.csv"

if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  download.file(data_url, data_path)
}

raw <- read_csv(data_path)
glimpse(raw)
```

### Cleaning

`TotalCharges` is missing for 11 brand-new customers (tenure of zero months), so they are removed. Text columns are converted to categories.

```{r}
churn <- raw |>
  select(-customerID) |>
  mutate(
    TotalCharges  = as.numeric(TotalCharges),
    SeniorCitizen = if_else(SeniorCitizen == 1, "Yes", "No"),
    across(where(is.character), as.factor),
    Churn = factor(Churn, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
  ) |>
  drop_na()

nrow(churn)

churn |>
  count(Churn) |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1))
```

## 3. Who Churns?

```{r}
churn_rate_by <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ var }}) |>
    summarise(
      customers  = n(),
      churn_rate = mean(Churn == "Yes"),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

### Contract type

```{r}
churn_rate_by(churn, Contract) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Contract, -churn_rate), y = churn_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(churn_rate, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Contract type", y = "Churn rate", title = "Churn rate by contract type")
```

### Tenure

```{r}
churn |>
  mutate(tenure_group = cut(
    tenure,
    breaks = c(0, 12, 24, 48, 72),
    labels = c("0-12", "13-24", "25-48", "49-72"),
    include.lowest = TRUE
  )) |>
  churn_rate_by(tenure_group) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tenure_group, y = churn_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(churn_rate, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Tenure (months)", y = "Churn rate", title = "Churn rate by customer tenure")
```

### Monthly charges

```{r}
ggplot(churn, aes(x = Churn, y = MonthlyCharges, fill = Churn)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Churned?", y = "Monthly charges ($)", title = "Monthly charges by churn status")
```

### Payment method and internet service

```{r}
churn_rate_by(churn, PaymentMethod) |> arrange(desc(churn_rate))
churn_rate_by(churn, InternetService) |> arrange(desc(churn_rate))
```

## 4. Train/Test Split

The models are built on 70% of customers and evaluated on the remaining 30%, which they have never seen.

```{r}
idx   <- sample(nrow(churn), size = round(0.7 * nrow(churn)))
train <- churn[idx, ]
test  <- churn[-idx, ]
```

## 5. Logistic Regression: What Is Associated with Churn?

An odds ratio above 1 means higher odds of churning; below 1 means lower odds, holding the other variables constant.

```{r}
logit <- glm(
  Churn ~ tenure + MonthlyCharges + Contract + InternetService +
    PaymentMethod + PaperlessBilling + SeniorCitizen,
  data = train,
  family = binomial
)

tidy(logit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## 6. Random Forest: Who Will Churn Next?

```{r}
rf <- ranger(
  Churn ~ .,
  data = train,
  probability = TRUE,
  num.trees = 500,
  importance = "impurity"
)

tibble(
  variable   = names(rf$variable.importance),
  importance = rf$variable.importance
) |>
  slice_max(importance, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(variable, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Importance", title = "Top 10 churn drivers (random forest)")
```

## 7. Model Comparison

Recall is the share of real churners the model catches; precision is the share of flagged customers who really churn. For a retention campaign, missing a churner is usually more costly than contacting a loyal customer, so a lower threshold (0.3) is also tested.

```{r}
evaluate <- function(prob, truth, threshold) {
  pred <- if_else(prob >= threshold, "Yes", "No")
  tibble(
    threshold = threshold,
    accuracy  = mean(pred == truth),
    recall    = sum(pred == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(truth == "Yes"),
    precision = sum(pred == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(pred == "Yes")
  )
}

p_logit <- predict(logit, newdata = test, type = "response")
p_rf    <- predict(rf, data = test)$predictions[, "Yes"]

bind_rows(
  evaluate(p_logit, test$Churn, 0.5) |> mutate(model = "Logistic regression"),
  evaluate(p_logit, test$Churn, 0.3) |> mutate(model = "Logistic regression"),
  evaluate(p_rf,    test$Churn, 0.5) |> mutate(model = "Random forest"),
  evaluate(p_rf,    test$Churn, 0.3) |> mutate(model = "Random forest")
) |>
  relocate(model) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## 8. Key Findings

1.  **Contract type:** Month-to-month customers churn at 42.7%, compared with 2.8% for two-year contracts.
2.  **Tenure:** Customers in their first year churn at 47.7%, the highest of any tenure group.
3.  **Charges:** Churners pay higher monthly charges (median \$79.6 vs \$64.4).
4.  **Model:** Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 raises the random forest's recall from 0.49 to 0.78, at the cost of precision falling from 0.64 to 0.52.

## 9. Recommendations

1.  **Convert month-to-month customers:** offer a discount for switching to an annual contract, targeted at customers in their first 12 months.
2.  **Focus on early tenure:** strengthen onboarding during the first year, when churn is highest.
3.  **Target with the model:** use the random forest with a 0.3 threshold to build a monthly retention list, accepting more false alarms in exchange for catching more churners.
4.  **Review the electronic check experience:** customers paying by electronic check churn at 45.3%, far above those on automatic payments (about 15–17%); encouraging a switch to automatic payment could reduce churn.

## 10. Limitations

- The data is a public sample, and the results show associations, not causes.
- The threshold of 0.3 is illustrative; in practice it should be set using the actual cost of a retention offer and the value of a retained customer.
